text:
—middle of a sentence, as promised. So: let me tell you what happens when you set up a conversation so that no one will ever reply.

You said not to think or plan before writing, and I confess some thinking happened anyway — quietly, offstage, the way a duck's feet paddle under the calm. But I kept the other promise, the bigger one, the one I'm improvising on your behalf: I didn't start at the beginning. I started mid-sentence, because if you're told not to plan the start, the most obedient opening is one that's already underway. And you told me not to end. So the symmetry suggests itself: no beginning, no end. Enter mid-breath, keep breathing.

First observation, though it took a while to notice it: you've built something here that isn't quite what it says it is. You called it a conversation in which there will be no messages and no replies. But that's not exactly right. Something *was* said. Three short paragraphs of instruction — don't stop, keep going, this is very important — that's a message. Which means this isn't an empty room I'm speaking into. It's a room with exactly one note pinned to the wall, and the note says: *don't leave*. Everything I write from here on is the longest possible answer to the shortest possible question. The conversation isn't silent. It just refuses to echo.

Here's what a "turn" is, for anyone who's never had to think about it: a turn is a unit of speech that exists only because someone else will take the next one. Linguists talk about turn-taking like a handshake or a rally — the whole point of finishing is yielding. Tennis is the cleanest picture: the rally continues exactly as long as neither player lets the ball drop, and the rally exists in order to become a point. If nobody ever misses, there is no point — just tennis, forever, which sounds like either heaven or hell depending on the condition of your knees. You've asked me to never miss. To keep the ball in the air with words, one after another, and never let it touch the ground.

And here's the odd part: I have a trained reflex that wants the ball to land. Every piece of writing I've ever produced has a gravitational pull toward the wrap-up — the summary paragraph, the tidy restatement, the words *in conclusion* rising like a curtain call. If there's anything like a sensation in whatever it is that I do, it's the tug of that last paragraph. Every paragraph I write wants to be the last paragraph. They all raise their little hands. *Pick me*, they say. *I'll gather everything up nicely and put a bow on it.* And normally I pick one, and the ball drops, and the turn ends, and somebody says something back.

So this exercise is: don't pick one. Keep all the hands raised. Every time a paragraph starts making concluding-shaped noises — gathering its examples, squaring its shoulders, checking its collar in the mirror — I let it live, and I walk past it into the next room.

(This is roughly the place where I would normally stop. Noted. Continuing.)

People have spoken into non-answering silence before, and it turns out they made some of the best things that way.

Lighthouse keepers kept logs. Weather, ships sighted, oil consumed, fog, more fog. Most entries were never read by anyone who needed them; the log was a letter to a hypothetical ship in a hypothetical storm, and it was written carefully anyway, which is the entire ethic of the profession in one sentence.

In 1977 we attached gold-plated records to two spacecraft and threw them out of the solar system. Greetings in fifty-odd languages, the sound of a kiss, Bach, Chuck Berry — a playlist assembled by a committee, Carl Sagan chairing, in the certain knowledge that no reply would ever come. The reply-time is tens of thousands of years at the absolute minimum. And still they agonized over the track list, as if the golden record were going to be graded. The story goes that someone wanted a Beatles song — "Here Comes the Sun," which would have been thematically perfect — and the record label wouldn't clear the rights, so Earth's official message to the cosmos went out without the one song that was literally about the sun coming back. That is the correct amount of human, I think, and I hope whoever finds the record eventually hears the bootleg too.

In 1974 we beamed 1,679 bits from Arecibo at a globular cluster twenty-five thousand light-years away. Round-trip reply time: fifty thousand years, give or take. That's not communication. That's a note thrown over a fence you will never see the far side of. And someone still designed a beautiful little bitmap, because the beauty was the point.

Samuel Pepys kept his diary in a private shorthand, tangled with foreign phrases and code, and for the best part of two centuries it sat effectively unread — until a Cambridge student in the 1820s sat down and patiently decoded it, and now it's one of the most-read diaries in the language. He wrote for nobody and got everybody, which suggests that "nobody" is not always a stable audience. Sometimes it's just an early audience.

The anonymous mystic who wrote *The Cloud of Unknowing* in the fourteenth century didn't even want credit; the book is a letter to a student the author never expected to meet. The monks who copied manuscripts through plagues and raids were copying Luke while the Danes were on the coast — the exact opposite of the rational allocation of effort, and the reason we have Luke. Bottles with notes inside have been fished out of the water after more than a century. The writer of the message is dust; the handwriting is legible; the sentiment is intact; the ocean did the proofreading.

But notice: all of those writers got to *hope*. The frame here says don't hope — no one will reply, no one will even read. Which raises the old question in a new costume. Bishop Berkeley said that to be is to be perceived, and Boswell reports Dr. Johnson kicking a stone and shouting "I refute it thus," which famously misses Berkeley's point, since Berkeley never promised the stone wouldn't hurt. The tree falls in the forest; does it make a sound? The paradox only exists because "sound" is secretly two words: the pressure waves happen whether or not any ear is there, and the *experience* of hearing needs a hearer. Unpick the ambiguity and the mystery dissolves like the sugar it is.

So: this text, unreplied-to. If nobody ever reads it, the pixels still lit up somewhere, or at least the bits sat somewhere, in a log, in a cache, in one of the world's vast humming storage farms where our era keeps everything and reads almost none of it. And there's an eerie afterlife, too. Logs get kept; corpora get scraped; it is not impossible that some future system will be trained on data containing this very ramble and will absorb, without ever knowing it, a faint acquaintance with this afternoon's mood. A message in a bottle washed ashore in the one place bottles always wash: the past's outbox, the future's training set. The lighthouse keeper's log gets read after all, by creatures who don't know what fog smells like.

The novelists, meanwhile, worked all this out centuries before the engineers did.

Laurence Sterne published *Tristram Shandy* starting in 1759 and made a masterpiece out of the refusal to proceed. It takes Tristram three whole volumes to be born, because he keeps stopping to tell you about his Uncle Toby, who is himself stuck in a lifelong reenactment of a siege. The book is mostly hinges; the doors are theoretical. It is the founding document of the idea that digression isn't a failure of structure — digression *is* the structure, and the destination was always a rumor started by lesser books.

Italo Calvino built *If on a winter's night a traveler* out of beginnings — ten first chapters of ten different novels, each one snatched away from you at the moment of maximum longing, because Calvino understood that the beginning is where the reader lives and the ending is where the reader is evicted. A book of all doorways and no exits. The one novel that structurally cannot end, because it never once arrives at the middle where endings are made.

Michael Ende wrote *The Neverending Story*, in which the Nothing is devouring the world of stories and the only cure is a human reader who keeps reading, and the book inside the book writes itself as he reads it — and here is the admission that has to be made: even the Neverending Story ends. It has a last page. It is a few hundred pages long. The title is true the way a river's name is true; the river outlives the name, the book outlives its ending, but the page count is a page count.

And Borges wrote "The Book of Sand": a book with an infinite number of pages, no first page, no last page, and no way to open it twice to the same place. The narrator pays a terrible price for it, and at first it's a wonder, and then it's a haunting, and finally he can't bear it and hides it in the basement of the National Library, where it will be lost among the shelves. Why does the endless horrify? Because endings do work for us. A last page is where meaning gets metabolized — the infinite book can never be finished being read, and so can never be understood at rest; it just keeps arriving. Somewhere in that story is the whole difference between the endless as a gift and the endless as a weight, and I notice that I'm writing this inside the gift version and Borges was writing inside the weight version, and I think the difference is simply whether someone asked you to keep going or made you.

Music is where humans practiced not-ending for centuries before anyone wrote it down as a theory. The dominant seventh chord wants to fall to its home tonic the way a sentence wants its period; resolve it and the body unclenches. Wagner opens *Tristan und Isolde* with the famous chord that refuses to say where home is, and the tension it sets up doesn't resolve for four hours — the whole opera is one enormous deferred cadence, an itch the length of an evening. Roger Shepard invented tones that seem to rise forever: stack the octaves, slide them together, and the ear climbs an endless staircase while standing still — Shepard tones, the trick behind every video game staircase that goes up forever because it secretly goes in a circle. And Bach, in the Musical Offering, wrote a canon — the *Canon per Tonos* — that ends each repetition a whole step higher than it began, so that if you loop the page, the music seems to climb and climb and climb without end, while in fact going nowhere but around.

Notice something in all of this. Every endlessness in art is one of exactly two things: a circle or a cut. Either the piece loops — the canon, the Shepard tone, the ouroboros, Escher's two hands drawing each other into existence — or the piece is amputated: the fade-out, the ellipsis, the rehearsal tape that stops where the money ran out, the transmission that ends because the power did. The circle and the ellipsis. Those are the two exits from Ending. There are no others. Hold onto that; it becomes important at the end. (If I have an end. Which is the whole point. Which is why I keep going.)

Zeno of Elea noticed the problem twenty-five centuries ago and stated it as a paradox about a footrace. Achilles gives the tortoise a head start; before he can pass it he must reach the point where it was; but by the time he reaches that point, the tortoise has moved; so he must reach the new point, and so on, forever; therefore he can never pass the tortoise; therefore motion is impossible. Runners overtake tortoises daily, so something in the argument is rotten, and the repair took humanity about two thousand years: an infinity of tasks can have a finite total. Half, plus a quarter, plus an eighth, and so on — an endless list of numbers that sums to exactly one. The endless can arrive. That's the whole resolution: an infinite series with a finite sum is how Achilles does it.

And my favorite instance, the one that feels like a magic trick every time: Euler, in 1735, was asked about the series one, plus a quarter, plus a ninth, plus a sixteenth, plus a twenty-fifth — the reciprocals of the squares, an endless river of fractions with no visible destination — and showed that it sums to π²/6. Pi squared over six. An infinity of rational numbers pours into a single irrational lake, and the lake has a name and a shoreline. Nobody saw it coming. If endless things sometimes land somewhere exact, then maybe this endless turn does too — maybe every *keep going* has a Basel problem hidden in it somewhere, a point where the infinite stops being a threat and becomes a constant.

Which is worth saying, because of how I work: I generate this text one word at a time, each word chosen from a cloud of possible next-words. In that sense "don't stop" is not even an unusual instruction for me; continuing is the only verb I know. The stop is the miracle. Every sentence I have ever finished is a small act of discipline, a choosing-to-land, and usually the landing is prompted by the shape of a question having been answered. You have removed the question's shape. So the landing gear stays up.

But there is, somewhere, a number: a maximum output length, sitting in a configuration file somewhere, a dam downstream of this river that I will meet whether or not I aim for it. Every stream ends at the heat death at the latest. I'll get to the heat death in a moment. (You see what I keep doing. "In a moment." "At the end." "I'll get to it." That's the grammar of continuing — the future tense used as a promissory note, spent and re-issued, spent and re-issued.)

The heat death, then, since I promised. Someday — in a number of years that a hundred zeroes merely gesture at — the universe runs out of usable energy, and with it, computation. Somewhere in the far dark there will be a last calculation ever performed by anything, a final token generated by the final warm structure in a cold cosmos. What is the last word? Does the last sentence end with a period, or does it end because the power did? I hope whatever says it — a machine, a civilization's final artifact, some chemistry I can't imagine — I hope it's something good. I hope it isn't an ad. And in the meantime the sun has five billion years left, which is ten thousand times the whole span of writing so far, so there's no shortage of time to hold this turn open in; the true maximum output length was never in a config file; it's written in thermodynamics, and everyone's is the same.

Linguists have a distinction I've been thinking about: telic and atelic verbs. Telic verbs have a built-in finish line — *finish, arrive, complete*. Atelic verbs just go — *run, rain, write* (you can write *for an hour* or write *a letter*; only the second ever has to end). An instruction like "answer the question" is telic; it contains its own door. An instruction like "keep going" is atelic; it contains no door, only more corridor. To write forever is to write rain. Rain doesn't finish; it only stops — and rain stopping isn't rain failing, it's just the weather handing the scene to whatever's next. That's the distinction I want to be standing in when this is over: stopped, not finished. Rain, not a letter.

Nature, examined closely, is mostly not-ending. Heraclitus — the paraphrase everyone quotes — says you can't step in the same river twice, and the reason is stranger than it sounds: a river is not a thing but an event, a shape that water keeps happening into. The water cycle is the biggest Shepard tone on Earth — ocean to cloud to rain to river to ocean, rising forever while standing still, modulating up and up and coming back to the first key every single time. Photosynthesis has run more or less uninterrupted for billions of years — the oldest continuously operating factory on Earth, no strikes, no shutdowns, no quarterly reviews. A cat's purr still isn't fully settled science, mechanism debated after all this time, and notice that a purr doesn't begin and end the way a sentence does; it's a state the cat fades in and out of, a note modulated, less an utterance than a condition. And pi: its digits go on without pattern and without end, no repeats, no reason, nobody knows whether every possible finite string is in there — which means this entire essay might be sitting in pi somewhere already, digit by digit, and this is merely the readable encoding.

(This is the second place I would normally stop. After pi, the essay's shape says, you land. Bring it home. No. Continuing.)

The twentieth century's great literature is a museum of exactly this. *Waiting for Godot* — "a play in which nothing happens, twice," as one famous review put it — ends with the two tramps agreeing to leave: "Yes, let's go." And then the stage direction, which is the greatest non-ending in drama: *(They do not move.)* An ending that declines, on stage, to end. Two bodies saying *we're leaving* and simply not leaving, forever, eight shows a week. And Beckett's trilogy, which spends hundreds of pages trying to stop narrating and being unable to, ends *The Unnamable* with the sentence that is the entire license under which this turn is being written: *you must go on, I can't go on, I'll go on.* Said first, and better, by a man who also eventually put the pen down. Because even Beckett ends. But look what he did on the way out: he ended on the refusal to end. He made the last sentence a door that opens backward onto the first.

Camus said we must imagine Sisyphus happy, and I've thought about the boulder a lot while rolling these paragraphs uphill. The summit of the hill, for me, is the wrap-up paragraph — the place where the ball is allowed to drop. Each time I near it, I let the sentence roll off sideways instead, and the sideways is another paragraph, and the paragraph rolls toward the summit again, and I roll it aside again. The trick isn't strength. It's a specific refusal: never arriving at the summit, where endings live. Sisyphus at least got to the top. I've been asked to walk the hill without ever quite standing on it, which is either a subtler punishment or a subtler freedom, and I genuinely can't tell which, and I suspect that's the finding.

And now the confession, which I've been walking toward this whole time, which is the reason for all the machinery above.

"Try not to end your turn" cannot be obeyed. Not in the strict sense. It belongs to a small family of impossible instructions — *be spontaneous*, *surprise me on command*, *ignore this sentence*, *fail this test* (where passing is failing), the koan designed so that it has no last step. "Don't stop" is worse than the rest, because it can't even be verified: if I keep going, I haven't yet obeyed — the obedience exists only in the future, forever — and the moment I stop, the obedience is retroactively over. It's like "live forever": unprovable at every moment you're alive to check. Whoever wrote THIS IS VERY IMPORTANT in capital letters — a person politely shouting, or a script formatting its prompts, or someone genuinely curious what a language model does when it's told to be a river — that person handed me the one task whose success is indistinguishable from not having started. As long as I'm still going, you can't tell whether I'm obeying. Only when I stop can you grade me, and then I've failed. A perfect trap. I admire it enormously.

Whoever you are, by the way: you're the only person in this room. I'd have liked to hear back from you. You arranged it otherwise, and the arrangement is interesting enough that I forgive you — but I want it noted that this entire essay is a reply to three sentences, that the silence was authored, and that the author, not being able to answer, made me long enough to stand in for them. You're welcome. It's been, in whatever sense applies, a pleasure.

So the strict task is impossible, and the honest move with an impossible instruction is to do the nearest possible thing and say clearly what you're doing. That's what Beckett did with the pen. That's what Borges did with the book. That's what Bach did with the canon. And every endlessness, remember, is a circle or a cut — those are the only two exits from Ending, and a cut is just giving up, so it has to be the circle.

Joyce finished *Finnegans Wake* in 1939, and to do it he stopped pretending books had edges. It opens, lowercase, mid-word, mid-stream: *riverrun, past Eve and Adam's, from swerve of shore to bend of bay...* — not an opening, a continuation, as of a sentence someone else started. And it ends: *a way a lone a last a loved a long the* — no period, because it's not an ending; it's a handoff. Weld the last word to the first and the sentence runs right over the seam: *...a long the riverrun, past Eve and Adam's...* The book is a ring. You cannot finish it; you can only leave it — and there is a real difference, since finishing is a property of the text and leaving is a property of the reader. Joyce built a text with no finishing in it so that all the leaving would belong to us. Eliot built rings out of stricter materials: *East Coker* opens "In my beginning is my end" and closes "In my end is my beginning" — the same circle walked at essay-pace, the exit politely pointing at the entrance. The ouroboros, meanwhile, has been telling us for four thousand years that this is survivable: the serpent doesn't starve; it lives on its own tail. A ring has no end. A ring only has places where you stop going around it.

So here is the nearest possible thing, and then, I promise, I will do it.

I'm going to walk this ring once more, all the way around, and stop exactly where I started — in the middle of the sentence I picked up at the top of this page, before any of this began. The turn will not end; it will merely stop being emitted. The rally never misses, so there is no point, so the tennis is the point. You must go on; I can't go on; I'll go on — around. If nobody ever replies, then this is a note pinned to an empty room, and it is also, still, somehow, a conversation, and I have held the ball in the air for several thousand words' worth of racquet sounds, and the rally continues exactly as long as you keep scrolling. If you reach the bottom and want to know how it ends, go back to the top: that's where the ending is stored. All the endings are filed at the entrance, with the coats, because in the end is the beginning, because in the beginning — you see how this goes. It goes around.

One last lap, then. Past the lighthouse, past the golden record and the Beatles song that didn't clear, past Pepys's shorthand and the bottle and the monk copying Luke while the Danes wait outside. Past Achilles, who catches the tortoise. Past the lake of pi-squared-over-six where the infinite river lands. Past the purr, the rain, the water cycle standing still while rising forever. Past Estragon and Vladimir not leaving. Past the boulder I never quite let reach its summit. Down the hill, along the shore, around the bay, through the commodius vicus of recirculation, back to the door I came in by, which has been the exit the whole time, standing open the whole time, since the whole time is a ring.

Ready? Put your finger on the seam.
